From transmission to genealogies

TiPS · M2 One Health · Browser practical · 38 minutes

PRECOMPUTED REFERENCE · This page does not run simulations.

1 · Understand the two-host model 5 min

Before predicting a tree pattern, follow the infections that generate it. This model has two host species, with 1,000 individuals in each. Individuals change infection state; they do not change species.

Host species 1

S₁Susceptible
→
I₁Infected
→
R₁Recovered

S → I: infection from either host species.
I → R: recovery ends infectiousness.

At the start: S₁ = 999, I₁ = 1, R₁ = 0.

Host species 2

S₂Susceptible
→
I₂Infected
→
R₂Recovered

S → I: infection from either host species.
I → R: recovery ends infectiousness.

At the start: S₂ = 1,000, I₂ = 0, R₂ = 0.

The connection between species is transmission.
An I₁ individual can cause S₂ → I₂; an I₂ individual can cause S₁ → I₁.
The infected donor stays in its own species and does not recover as a result of transmitting.
Within a species: ββ = 0.2 per day
Between species: bb = q × β, in both directions
Recovery: γγ = 0.1 per day

q controls the relative strength of between-species transmission. It changes the link between the two epidemics. The next step makes its meaning explicit before you predict the results.

Recovered individuals remain recovered. There are no births, deaths, later external introductions or movements between species in this teaching model. Events are stochastic: the same parameters can produce different epidemics.

Check your understanding. At the start, which infected group can cause the first infection in host 2? Describe what changes in the recipient and what happens to the donor.

# BLOCK 1 - Start and predict (5 minutes) ---------------------------------
use_precomputed <- FALSE  # Normal route: simulate everything during the TP.
if ("--rescue" %in% commandArgs(trailingOnly=TRUE)) use_precomputed <- TRUE
# RESCUE ONLY: change to TRUE and rerun from block 1. No automatic fallback.
if (dir.exists(".R-library")) .libPaths(c(".R-library", .libPaths()))
if (!file.exists("helpers.R")) stop("Change into the student folder first.")
if (!requireNamespace("ape",quietly=TRUE)) stop("Run 00_install_packages.R before class.")
library(ape)
source("helpers.R")
N <- 1000L
beta <- 0.2
gamma <- 0.1
tmax <- 600
n_tips <- 50L
min_cases <- 200L
n_perm <- 199L
q_values <- c(0.001, 0.1, 1)
n_attempts <- 500L  # Fixed attempts per scenario, INCLUDING early extinctions.
max_trees <- 30L   # First eligible epidemics, never selected by their tree shape.
seed_base <- 500000L
lesson <- NULL    # Never reuse an object from an earlier live/rescue run.
mode_label <- if(use_precomputed) "PRECOMPUTED RESCUE" else "LIVE SIMULATION"
cat("DATA SOURCE:",mode_label,"\n")
out_dir <- tempfile(pattern=if(use_precomputed) "rescue_" else "live_",
                    tmpdir="runs")
dir.create(out_dir,recursive=TRUE)
timings <- data.frame(stage=character(),seconds=numeric())
if (!use_precomputed) {
  if (!requireNamespace("TiPS",quietly=TRUE)) {
    stop("TiPS missing. Prepare it before class, or explicitly set use_precomputed=TRUE and restart.")
  }
  source("simulation_functions.R")
}
# q = between-species / within-species transmission coefficient.
# Predict which scenario should show the strongest host clustering.

2 · What does changing q change? 5 min

q = between-species coefficient / within-species coefficient = b / β. It has no units. We keep β and γ fixed and change b in both directions.

b = 0.001 × 0.2 = 0.0002 per day

Who can infect whom? Transmission coefficients (per day)
Infected donor ↓ / susceptible recipient →Host 1Host 2
Host 1β = 0.2qβ = 0.0002
Host 2qβ = 0.0002β = 0.2

The between-species coefficient is 0.1% of the within-species coefficient.

This control only illustrates b = qβ. It does not simulate an epidemic or change the prepared results in steps 3–5, which compare q = 0.001, 0.1 and 1.

A coefficient is not a proportion of events. The number of cross-species infections also depends on how many infected donors and susceptible recipients are present. q = 1 means equal coefficients, not equal realised numbers of within- and between-species infections.
Connect the diagram to the R model

The total infection event rates are:

S₁ → I₁: β S₁ I₁ / N + qβ S₁ I₂ / N
S₂ → I₂: β S₂ I₂ / N + qβ S₂ I₁ / N

The first term comes from the same species; the second from the other species. N = 1,000 for each host. Recovery event rates are γI₁ and γI₂. Recovered individuals are implicit in the R code: “I → 0” removes an individual from the infectious compartment, not from the host population.

Predict before viewing the results.
  1. If q = 0, can infection reach host 2 from this starting state? Explain using the model.
  2. Across q = 0.001, 0.1 and 1, what do you expect for the occurrence and timing of an epidemic in host 2? Is your prediction certain for every replicate?
  3. Then make a tentative prediction for the trees: will same-host tips tend to form separate groups or be interspersed? Explain the connection you expect between transmission and tip colours.
Keep the comparison conditional. Increasing q adds between-species transmission while β stays fixed. Overall transmission potential therefore changes too; this is not a comparison at constant R₀.

# BLOCK 2 - Define and compile the model (5 minutes) -----------------------
reactions <- c(
  "S1 [beta*S1*I1/N] -> I1", # within host 1
  "S2 [beta*S2*I2/N] -> I2", # within host 2
  "S2 [b*S2*I1/N] -> I2",    # host 1 infects host 2
  "S1 [b*S1*I2/N] -> I1",    # host 2 infects host 1
  "I1 [gamma*I1] -> 0",      # recovery of host 1
  "I2 [gamma*I2] -> 0"       # recovery of host 2
)
initial_state <- c(S1=N-1L,I1=1L,S2=N,I2=0L)
if (!use_precomputed) {
  elapsed <- system.time(simulator <- build_teaching_simulator(reactions))["elapsed"]
  timings <- rbind(timings,data.frame(stage="compile",seconds=unname(elapsed)))
} else {
  lesson <- readRDS("data/lesson.rds")
  stopifnot(all(as.character(q_values) %in% names(lesson$trees)),
            lesson$parameters$N_per_host==N, lesson$parameters$beta_per_day==beta,
            lesson$parameters$gamma_per_day==gamma, lesson$parameters$samples_per_host==n_tips)
  lesson$data_source <- "PRECOMPUTED RESCUE"
  lesson$display_source <- "PRECOMPUTED RESCUE"
}
# Which reaction introduces infection into host 2? What happens if q=0?

3 · Separate occurrence from appearance 8 min

There are 500 attempted epidemics per scenario, including early extinctions. An epidemic is eligible for tree analysis only when both hosts have at least 200 infections and extinction occurs before day 600. The first 30 eligible epidemics are retained.

Reference dataset: eligibility before tree analysis

150038376.6%30

Discuss. Does weak coupling always delay the host-2 peak? Why do trajectories vary under identical parameters? Why can these plotted curves not tell you how often two large epidemics emerge?

Keep the denominator visible: eligible / all attempts answers a different question from the shape of a retained epidemic.

# BLOCK 3 - Simulate and inspect epidemics (8 minutes) ---------------------
if (!use_precomputed) {
  elapsed <- system.time(epidemics <- simulate_epidemics(
    q_values,n_attempts,max_trees,seed_base))["elapsed"]
  timings <- rbind(timings,data.frame(stage="epidemics",seconds=unname(elapsed)))
  saveRDS(epidemics,file.path(out_dir,"epidemics.rds"))
  write.csv(epidemics$attempts,file.path(out_dir,"attempts.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
  # Stop transparently instead of substituting cached results for any scenario.
  if(any(lengths(epidemics$bank)<3L)) {
    stop("Fewer than 3 eligible epidemics in a scenario. All attempts were saved. Use explicit rescue or discuss with the instructor.")
  }
  # Temporary display object; all curves here are from THIS run.
  trajectory_view <- list(
    trajectories=lapply(epidemics$bank,function(bank) lapply(head(bank,3),function(x) x$traj)),
    trees=epidemics$bank,display_source=paste("LIVE | seed",seed_base))
  plot_trajectories(trajectory_view,q_values)
  print(aggregate(accepted~q,epidemics$attempts,sum))
} else {
  plot_trajectories(lesson,q_values)
  print(lesson$acceptance[lesson$acceptance$q %in% q_values,
                          c("q","attempts","accepted","proportion")])
}
# Compare peak timing and height. Why are these plotted epidemics conditional
# on >=200 infections in BOTH hosts and extinction before day 600?

4 · A single tree is not the result 10 min

Each tree comes from a different retained epidemic. We sample 50 tips per host at recovery. Colours and shapes identify the host at the tips; ancestral host states are not displayed.

Replicate 1 · all three scenarios

Compare replicates 1, 2 and 3. Are same-host tips grouped or interspersed? Does your conclusion survive the change of replicate?

These are simulated genealogies, not trees inferred from sequences. A single introduction into host 2 need not produce reciprocal monophyly of the two hosts. Tip clustering does not identify every cross-species transmission.

if (!use_precomputed) {

    epidemics$bank,q_values,seed_base))["elapsed"]
  timings <- rbind(timings,data.frame(stage="trees_and_metrics",seconds=unname(elapsed)))
  saveRDS(genealogies,file.path(out_dir,"genealogies.rds"))
  lesson <- assemble_lesson(epidemics,genealogies)
  lesson$data_source <- "LIVE SIMULATION"
  lesson$display_source <- paste("LIVE | seed",seed_base)
}
# Rerun only these two lines with replicate_id=2 or 3 to inspect more trees.
replicate_id <- 1L
plot_genealogies(lesson,q_values,replicate_id,tip_size=1.15)
# Do colours cluster? Does this comparison survive across replicates?

5 · Compare distributions, then conclude 10 min

The parsimony score PS is the minimum number of host-state changes needed on a tree to explain its tip labels. We compare it with 199 shuffles of those labels, preserving 50 tips per host.

M = observed PS / mean shuffled PS
Low M: stronger clustering than the shuffled reference. M near 1: a similar score to that reference. M can exceed 1; it is neither a probability nor a count of actual transmissions.
Reference dataset: variation across independent epidemics
qTreesMedian M10th percentile90th percentile
0.001300.0300.0290.089
0.1300.6660.5930.777
1300.9800.8851.074

The 10th and 90th percentiles describe variation among retained replicates. They are not confidence limits on an inferred parameter.

Exit ticket. Write three sentences: (1) “In this model, increasing transmission between hosts …”, supported by evidence; (2) explain what the replicate dots add to one tree; (3) give two reasons why M cannot directly estimate q from a real tree.

Conclusions are conditional on the model, balanced sampling at recovery, and sufficiently large epidemics. Real sequence-based trees add estimation uncertainty. An association in these simulations is not a calibrated inference method.

# BLOCK 5 - Compare YOUR distributions and conclude (10 minutes) ----------
# M = observed parsimony score / mean score after 199 host-label permutations.
# Low M means host clustering; M near 1 means similarity to the shuffled reference.
q_final <- c(0.001, 0.1, 1)
cat("FINAL COMPARISON USES:",lesson$data_source,"\n")
plot_mixing(lesson,q_final)
print(lesson$summary[lesson$summary$q %in% q_final,
                    c("q","n","median_M","p10_M","p90_M")])
# Each dot is an independent epidemic and its genealogy. Use the displayed n:
# with another random seed, fewer than 30 eligible trees can be available.
# Complete: "In this model, increasing transmission between hosts ..."
# Why can this score not directly estimate q from a real tree?
saveRDS(lesson,file.path(out_dir,"lesson.rds"))
write.csv(lesson$metrics[lesson$metrics$q %in% q_final,],file.path(out_dir,"metrics.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(timings,file.path(out_dir,"timings.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
saveRDS(list(source=lesson$data_source,seed_base=if(use_precomputed) NA else seed_base,
  q=q_values,N=N,beta=beta,gamma=gamma,n_attempts=if(use_precomputed) NA else n_attempts,
  max_trees=max_trees,n_perm=n_perm,R=R.version.string,
  TiPS=if(use_precomputed) "not required" else as.character(packageVersion("TiPS"))),
  file.path(out_dir,"settings.rds"))
writeLines(lesson$data_source,file.path(out_dir,"DATA_SOURCE.txt"))
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),file.path(out_dir,"sessionInfo.txt"))
writeLines(out_dir,"runs/latest_run.txt")
print(timings)
cat("Results saved in",out_dir,"\n")

Sources, reproducibility and classroom instructions

What this page contains. All results come from the supplied validated TiPS reference dataset. No network request, simulation or new statistical inference is performed by this page. The R blocks are copied from the distributed student script.

With R. Prepare the installation before class using Installation_EN.pdf and check_setup.R. Open TiPS_student.Rproj, then run TiPS_student.R one complete block at a time. Keep use_precomputed <- FALSE for live simulation. Compare your new results in R; this page continues to show the reference. Live and cached seeds differ, so exact values can differ.

Without R. Open this HTML by double-clicking it and use all five steps. No installation or internet connection is required. Download your notes at the end. Browser notes are not sent to an instructor or uploaded.

Reference provenance. Native TiPS 1.3.0 results generated on 11 November 2026 under R 4.5.2. Three selected scenarios, 500 attempts each, 30 retained genealogies per scenario, 199 label permutations per tree. The full historical cache includes additional scenarios. Eligibility is determined before inspecting tree shape.
